background: This person is a Middle Eastern man with a felony conviction (possession, non-violent, class one felony) from about seven years ago. He has gone back to school and earned a degree, aiming for corporate or professional work. He is currently starting his own event planning business (transportation, hotel arrangements) while continuing his education.
self_view_of_problem: He frames the problem as his criminal history blocking him from becoming 'a good productive member of society' and causing overwhelming frustration, anger, and depression because employers overlook him despite his qualifications. He sees it as a 'life sentence' that makes him consider 'going back to what I know' (crime/destructive behavior).
resistance_drivers: Believes that disclosing his felony upfront will lead to immediate rejection ('Probably get booted out right away'), making him reluctant to do so.
Feels that jobs willing to hire felons are 'dead end jobs' or not worth his degree and aspirations ('not the sort of jobs that I really wanna be doing').
Perceived systemic barriers: sees the expungement process as nearly impossible (requires governor's clemency) and finds advocacy groups politically charged, racially biased, or unhelpful.
Believes success depends heavily on 'who you know' in a politically charged city with scarce jobs, which feels out of his control.

ambivalence.for_change: He wants to stay on the right path, be productive, and use his degree for professional work. He is actively trying solutions: going to school, starting his own business, researching expungement and advocacy groups, and considering tactical disclosure to avoid wasted hope.
ambivalence.against_change: He is tempted to 'go back to what I know' (crime/using) because the rejection is so discouraging and low-wage jobs are unsustainable ('you can only work for $5, $6, $7 an hour for so long'). He is protecting his hope and avoiding further frustration by sometimes withholding disclosure until late in the process.

values_and_stakes: Being a 'good productive member of society' and using his education for meaningful work.
Honesty (he believes in disclosing his record, even when it costs him jobs).
Staying clean from his former lifestyle and maintaining his rehabilitation.
His mental health and composure ('if I'm not okay here... I don't stand a chance').
His self-owned business and entrepreneurial independence.

The conviction is expungable only via governor's clemency/pardon, not sealing.
He has a degree and wants corporate/professional work.
He interviews well and often feels a job is offered midway through, but rejection occurs after background check disclosure.
He has run his own background check to see what is reported.
He has been clean from substance abuse and crime for seven years.
He is starting an event planning business (transportation, hotel bookings).
He lives in a politically charged city where he believes jobs go to people who know people.
He has researched advocacy groups for felons but found them unhelpful or biased.
He mentions the 9/11 attacks led many companies to implement blind background check policies.
